headline: Will Amutse pay for cement merger error? – IPC’s Hengombe
body: Independent Patriots for Change (IPC) parliamentarian Ferdinand Hengombe is demanding to know whether industries, mines and energy minister Modestus Amutse will be held liable for costs arising from his decision to overturn the Namibian Competition Commission’s rejection of the proposed Cheetah Cement and Ohorongo Cement merger. Hengombe raised the matter through questions tabled in the National Assembly on Wednesday, following a recent High Court judgment which found Amutse’s decision unlawful and invalid. The competition commission had initially rejected the proposed merger after finding that it could negatively affect competition in Namibia’s cement industry. Hengombe questioned why a minister would overturn a decision taken by a statutory body established specifically to regulate competition. “Why do we create entities funded by taxpayers’ money with particular responsibilities only to overturn them?” he asked. He questioned whether Amutse would be personally liable for any unnecessary costs incurred by the government as a result of the decision. Hengombe said the minister’s intervention undermined the mandate of the competition commission and raised concerns about accountability when ministerial decisions are later found to be unlawful. He said the minister should explain whether the government incurred legal or other costs as a result of the decision and whether any steps will be taken to recover such costs. Amutse is expected to respond next Thursday.

headline: Minister Indileni Daniel launches probe into NWR operations
body: The Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism has launched an investigation into the state-owned Namibia Wildlife Resorts’ alleged financial mismanagement, poor governance and unfair labour practices. The investigation includes establishing why some workers are still camping 11 months after a deadly blaze that destroyed most of their houses at Sesriem in the Namib-Naukluft National Park in the Hardap region. This comes amid politicians’ growing concerns about the company’s operations, and demands for a turnaround strategy. Environment minister Indileni Daniel appointed investigators, including a chairperson, from different departments within the ministry at the beginning of August to probe the parastatal’s affairs. The minister has been raising concerns since last year. In a letter dated 14 July 2025, Daniel expressed concern that she had received no formal reports from the NWR board on the company’s operations, governance or financial health. She wrote that she had not been provided the company’s annual budget, latest audited financial statements or an integrated strategic business plan. “I have received no formal reports from the board of directors concerning the operations, governance, or financial health of Namibia Wildlife Resorts (NWR). I must convey my deep disappointment in the board’s performance and its apparent failure to execute its fiduciary and oversight responsibilities,” the letter states. According to sources within the ministry, several agreements and transactions at the centre of the allegations include a Sun Karros agreement, an About Africa concession, an Enercon fuel agreement, and Haliburg Group and Alensy agreements. The probe will also examine the controversial Sesriem shuttle matter, as well as the matter concerning employees who were victims of a deadly blaze at Sesriem that destroyed their houses and killed a toddler (2). The workers are allegedly still staying in tents, 11 months after the incident. Other matters sources close to the investigation have raised include labour issues, financial mismanagement and the alleged abuse of company resources. Daniel in the letter says she has received no formal report from the NWR board on the company’s annual budget, latest audited financial statements or an integrated strategic business plan. “ . . . fundamental instruments that guide operations and ensure accountability in line with governance and regulatory frameworks. The absence of these documents indicates not only non-compliance but a concerning lack of financial and operational oversight,” she says. ‘OPERATIONAL PARALYSIS’ The minister describes the situation as putting NWR in a state of “operational paralysis”. The investigation comes as NWR continues to face questions over the treatment of employees and guests affected by the November 2025 fire. Environment ministry officials yesterday confirmed ongoing investigations. “Yes, we are aware of the investigations that are ongoing, however, we cannot divulge anything at the moment because it is an internal matter. If the story comes out it will make NWR put their books in order before our investigation, so we cannot alert them,” one official said. The investigation is expected to determine whether weaknesses in NWR’s governance and management systems contributed to the problems facing the company, including allegations of negligence, mismanagement and the possible abuse of company resources. The minister’s letter also questioned the absence of key financial and strategic documents, warning that the lack of such information indicated a “concerning lack of financial and operational oversight.” Questions sent to NWR caretaker and acting managing director Margaret Gustavo were not answered by the time of going to print. The move has been welcomed by Independent Patriots for Change shadow minister for environment and tourism Rodrick Likando, who says the investigation is long overdue. He says the party had repeatedly raised concerns about NWR’s financial challenges through parliamentary questions and motions. “NWR manages some of Namibia’s most valuable tourism assets, including lodges, national parks and other facilities. However, we have a problem with NWR because of the continuous financial challenges facing the company.” He says the quality of NWR service continues to deteriorate, which had been brought to the minister’s attention. “We really need an assessment of NWR facilities to determine how much funding is required to maintain and reconstruct some of these facilities. NWR continues to rely on the government. “Every now and then, funds are allocated, but we do not see the return on investment. So, we really welcome the minister’s decision to investigate the matter,” he says. Regarding the fire victims, Likando says the ministry needs to either assist them with relocation or being compensated. TURNAROUND STRATEGY Likando says the state-owned wildlife resorts company needs a turnaround strategy through the ministry to be able to carry out its mandate. “You cannot manage state resources and state assets in a way that the government does not make a profit because these are government companies. “We have a lot of stakeholders who have invested in tourism in Namibia, and they can also be requested to assist. “The minister could even establish some sort of fund to assist these people, and non-government organisations could come in and provide assistance.” He says the minister should be held accountable for the leadership at NWR. “We cannot continue to appoint managing directors on an acting basis, because whoever comes in, comes with their strategic plan. Then, when they leave, whoever comes in again will not follow that strategic plan and will come with another one,” he says.

headline: Dutch company to restart Sperrgebiet diamond mine
body: Dutch private equity investor Kenzoll Capital has partnered with MSF Commercials to restart operations at the Sperrgebiet Diamond Mine, formerly known as the Elizabeth Bay mine, near Lüderitz. Kenzoll has committed more than US$10 million (about N$170 million) to Namibia previously, with the latest partnership expected to bring the mine back into production after being largely inactive for the past eight years. The mine’s licences cover 245 364 hectares of the Sperrgebiet and hold estimated onshore diamond resources of 6.3 million carats and offshore resources of 4.2 million carats. The partnership will initially focus on restarting diamond operations, while also exploring opportunities to extract heavy mineral sands and critical metals from the mining licences. Following regulatory approvals, the total investment is expected to reach US$50 million (about N$850 million) as exploration and production of other minerals expand. “This partnership is part of our long-term commitment and investment in Namibia, with diamonds as the starting point and critical minerals to follow,” says Kenzoll Capital chief executive Corné Melissen.

headline: Zambezi region to host Miss Namibia 2027
body: SYMBOLIC HANDOVER … Omaheke governor Pijoo Nganate, as the previous host of Miss Namibia and Miss Teen Namibia 2026, symbolically handed over the crown to Zambezi governor Dorothy Kabula-Simushi as the incoming host of the national beauty pageants. Photo: Lugeretzia Kooper The Zambezi region has been chosen as the region to host the prestigious Miss Namibia 2027 national beauty pageant. The announcement of the hosting region ceremony, spearheaded by Namibian Broadcasting Corporation (NBC), was launched by Zambezi governor Dorothy Kabula-Simushi at Katima Mulilo on Tuesday. Omaheke governor Pijoo Nganate, as the previous host of Miss Namibia and Miss Teen Namibia 2026, symbolically handed over the crown to Kabula-Simushi as the incoming host of the national beauty pageants. Kabula-Simushi expressed her gratitude for being chosen as the next hosting region, saying Miss Namibia is a significant national platform that brings Namibians together. The region is strategically located, being the gateway to Zambia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Angola. “These strategic locations, combined with our natural beauty and cultural diversity, make the Zambezi region a fitting destination for an event of this nature. Miss Namibia 2027 will provide us with an opportunity to bring our heritage to the national stage and allow Namibians from all corners of the country and world to experience our rich cultural heritage,” she said. She added that the national beauty pageant will bring many opportunities for the local youth, as they will participate to gain experience, build networks and showcase their talent. Kabula-Simushi called upon the local business community, corporate partners and entrepreneurs to come forward to support Miss Namibia 2027. “The support varies from accommodation, transportation for finalists, hospitality, catering venues and beauty and fashion services,” she said. “We want Miss Namibia 2027 to make a lasting impact for the Zambezi region. Most importantly, we want the people of the Zambezi region to feel proud to host Miss Namibia 2027. Beyond infrastructure facilities, we have something that cannot be measured in monetary terms, and that is the warm hospitality of the people of the Zambezi region,” Kabula-Simushi said. NBC board of directors vice chairperson Oaitse van Staden says hosting Miss Namibia 2027 will create opportunities for local performing artists, musicians, dancers, designers, photographers, make-up artists, stylists, event managers, creative practitioners and young entrepreneurs who will participate in one of the country’s most prominent national events. “Miss Namibia is not only an entertainment event. It is also an economic and creative-industry platform. We will be showcasing the Zambezi region itself, its people, its culture, its tourism potential, its businesses, its creativity and its unique contribution to the Namibian story,” she says.

headline: Nust explores alternatives for lab science students
body: The Namibia University of Science and Technology (Nust) says it is offering affected medical laboratory sciences students options to transfer to other programmes or partner institutions as it works to address accreditation challenges. In an update on Wednesday, the university said it was engaging independent laboratories to secure additional practical training placements for students pursuing the bachelor of medical laboratory sciences. The statement follows a 30 September release outlining challenges involving practical training capacity for work-integrated learning (WIL), laboratory facilities and professional supervision. Nust said it had met students individually to explain how the situation affects them, discuss their preferred academic options and identify the support each one requires. The university said it had consulted the Namibia Qualifications Authority on the validation and authentication of potential receiving institutions. It did not name those institutions or specify how many students were affected. Nust said financial arrangements would be determined individually and communicated directly to students once consultations were complete. “Individual students have been affected by the matter in different ways,” the university said. It said psychosocial support was available to help affected students cope with the situation, and that each student would receive written information about their case once consultations had concluded. Nust said it continues to keep the Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sport, Arts and Culture informed of developments. The university said it takes responsibility for finding solutions and would communicate directly with students as arrangements are finalised.

headline: Construction industry backs court decision on cement
body: The Construction Industries Federation (CIF) says protecting competition in the cement sector is key to protecting the construction industry. This comes after a High Court decision earlier this week reversed industries minister Modestus Amutse’s decision to allow a merger between Namibia’s two cement companies. “[CIF’s] position has always been that cement is too important to Namibia’s construction sector and infrastructure development to be considered only as a commercial transaction between parties,” CIF chief executive Bärbel Kirchner said on Monday. Whale Rock Cement, which owns the brand Cheetah Cement, had applied to the Namibian Competition Commission (NaCC) last year to purchase Schwenk Namibia’s shares in Ohorongo Cement. The competition watchdog prohibited the merger on the grounds that it would lead to monopoly in the cement sector. Whale Rock appealed the decision to the minister, who overturned the NaCC’s ruling. CIF then joined a court case with iTE Products to challenge that ruling in the High Court, on the basis that Amutse had not considered representations against the merger. “CIF did so in line with its mandate to represent the wider construction industry, given the potential implications of the transaction for contractors, small and medium enterprises, suppliers, public procurement, infrastructure delivery, employment and end-users,” the federation said on Monday. The High Court ruled that Amutse had not considered objections lodged with him against the merger. The minister admitted that the objections had never reached his desk. NaCC’s prohibition of the merger, therefore, remains in place. “CIF notes the court’s ruling and welcomes the clarity it provides on this important matter. The broader public interest, competition, fair access, employment and long-term construction capacity must remain central considerations,” Kirchner said.

headline: Venaani calls for emergency FMD relief for farmers
body: Popular Democratic Movement president McHenry Venaani has called on the government to introduce an emergency relief package for farmers affected by the current foot-and-mouth disease outbreak. Venaani raised this concern in the National Assembly on Wednesday, asking prime minister Elijah Ngurare what measures the government was taking to assist farmers facing financial difficulties as a result of the outbreak. “Water is being cut, and farmers are asked to pay the Namibia Revenue Agency (Namra). Is the government going to consider an emergency package?” Venaani asked. He said farmers affected by movement restrictions and disruptions to livestock markets were facing mounting financial pressure, and called for urgent government intervention. Venaani also referred to the recent announcement by Beefcor that it is considering retrenching about 393 workers, warning that the FMD crisis could have wider consequences for the meat industry and workers whose livelihoods depend on it. He questioned whether the government could consider giving affected businesses and farmers temporary relief from some of their financial obligations. “Is the government going to consider, because you are the head of government? Water is being cut, and farmers are asked to pay Namra,” he said. Venaani further called for Namra to ease its demands on affected farmers and businesses, while urging Beefcor and other companies not to move too quickly with retrenchments while the crisis persists. Venaani said the government should consider measures that would help farmers and businesses survive the disruption and protect jobs. The FMD outbreak has placed additional pressure on livestock producers, with restrictions on the movement and sale of cattle affecting operations and cash flow across the affected areas, he added. Venaani said the government’s response should therefore go beyond disease control and include measures to cushion farmers, businesses and workers from the economic impact of the outbreak. National Assembly speaker Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila, however, advised that the prime minister address the issues through a ministerial statement.

headline: Astronaut challenges pupils to dream bigger
body: Meeting someone who has seen earth from space was more than just an ordinary school visit for pupils at the Deutsche Höhere Privatschule Windhoek (DHPS). European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Matthias Maurer visited the school on Friday, giving pupils an opportunity to hear first-hand about life aboard the International Space Station (ISS), space exploration and the journey to becoming an astronaut. “It’s not every day that someone who has already seen our planet from space walks through our school gates. He answered their questions and shared experiences beyond learning from a textbook,” the school says in a statement issued yesterday. Maurer, who is the 600th person to travel into space and the fourth German to undertake a spacewalk, spent 177 days aboard the ISS during his Cosmic Kiss mission. He travelled more than 120 million kilometres, circling earth 2 832 times while conducting scientific experiments and living in weightlessness. “Although his achievements are undoubtedly impressive, it was above all his personality that captivated pupils,” the school says. For the pupils, it was not only his achievements in space that captured their attention, it says. Maurer spoke openly about his journey and the importance of curiosity, ambition and teamwork in achieving seemingly distant goals. He also shared insights into the preparation required for space missions and what everyday life is like aboard the ISS. “During his Cosmic Kiss mission aboard the ISS, he worked on scientific experiments, lived in weightlessness for months and looked down on our planet day after day from a perspective that very few people are privileged to experience,” DHPS says. It says Maurer encouraged pupils to dream bigger, adding that major achievements often begin with curiosity and the willingness to pursue a dream. According to the statement, pupils asked about space exploration, science and technology, and the earth’s future. “The interaction turned the visit into more than a presentation about space travel, exposing pupils to the possibilities created by science, technology and international cooperation,” DHPS says. Maurer is looking towards the next chapter of human space exploration, with an ambition to participate in the planned Artemis mission to the moon and represent Europe on the journey. DHPS says the visit demonstrated how encounters with people from different fields can encourage young people to think beyond what they already know and consider possibilities beyond their immediate surroundings. DHPS thanked Maurer, the ESA and the German embassy in Windhoek for making the visit possible. Maurer came to Namibia on 1 October and will stay for a 10-day tour aimed at strengthening scientific ties between Namibia and Europe and inspiring young people to explore careers in science, technology and innovation. He is participating in the country’s World Space Week commemoration, which kicked off on Monday and ends on Friday. He is expected to engage with about 8 000 pupils in Windhoek, Swakopmund, Ongwediva and Oshakati. He delivered a key note at the opening of the World Space Week in Windhoek on Monday.

headline: Training puts farmers’ field schools in focus
body: About 45 agricultural extension and forestry officers on Monday started a six-day training programme at Oshakati on the farmers’ field schools (FFS) concept. The training forms part of the Drylands Sustainable Landscapes Impact Project (DSL-IP), which plans to establish field schools in three landscapes in northern Namibia. The officers are from the Kunene-Cuvelai, Kavango and Etosha landscapes of the Mopane-Miombo Belt. DSL-IP national coordinator Reinhold Kambuli says the training aims to equip agricultural extension and forestry officers with skills to introduce the FFS concept to rural communities. Communities in the three landscapes are also being trained to run field schools. Their work will be supported by agricultural extension and forestry officers, whose existing work is similar to what the programme seeks to achieve. “At the moment, agricultural extension and forestry officers are extremely stressed due to limited resources. “So, the project is simply trying to complement the government’s efforts so the officers understand the FFS concept,” Kambuli says. He says the project plans to establish 220 field schools across the three landscapes, reaching about 7 200 people. “Each FFS should have 30 farmers,” he says. A FFS is not a conventional school. Farmers learn in the field through practical activities involving crops, soil, water and other natural resources. The schools aim to help communities address challenges such as land degradation, water scarcity, climate change and biodiversity loss, while improving agricultural production. The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), with funding from the Global Environment Facility, has signed an agreement with the International Institute for Rural Reconstruction (IIRR) to support the establishment of the schools. Two experts have been appointed through the partnership to assist the project. Speaking at the training on Monday, FAO Namibia officer in charge Ferdinand Mwapopi called on participants to strengthen their facilitation skills and focus on practical solutions that communities can adopt and sustain. He said the partnership with IIRR aims to establish functioning field schools in the three landscapes and build a network of community-based facilitators. Mwapopi said the IIRR will support the project in six areas: strategic alignment and preparation, landscape planning using the land degradation neutrality lens, capacity development, implementation, evaluation and reporting. The DSL-IP is jointly implemented by the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform and the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism. The project is being implemented in 11 countries across Africa and Asia. In Namibia, it was launched in March 2023 and is expected to run until April 2028.

headline: FMD derails Namibia’s El Niño plans
body: The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Namibia has forced the government to reconsider plans to support the livestock sector should Namibia be hit by the prevailing El Niño climate pattern. The pattern, which occurs every two to seven years, is a natural climate pattern caused by the unusual warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It could contribute to hotter and drier conditions in Namibia. Last month, the Namibia Meteorological Service said it expects El Niño conditions to strengthen from October, potentially bringing a hotter and drier than normal rainy season. Ben Haraseb, the director of the Directorate of Agricultural Production, Extension and Engineering Services at the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform, says the foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) outbreak has changed the situation. “At this moment, everything we had planned for the livestock sector when it comes to El Niño is out of the window because of the FMD outbreak,” Haraseb said at a recent dialogue on nutrition for growth, food security and sustainable agriculture. He says the government will now have to reconsider its plans. “We have to go back to the drawing board now,” Haraseb says. Namibia confirmed the current FMD outbreak last month, with the disease spreading to farms in the ||Kharas region. The outbreak has disrupted livestock sales, including auctions, making it difficult for farmers to reduce their herds in preparation of possible dry conditions. Percy Chimwamurombe, the head of the biology, chemistry and physics department at the Namibia University of Science and Technology, says the outbreak has made destocking difficult. “It’s a disaster. Not much can be done regarding that aspect for now, and we don’t know when we’re going to be able to engage in livestock sales,” he says. Chimwamurombe says cheaper sources of protein, including plant-based options, could be considered while the livestock sector is faced with these challenges. Tino Hess from German development agency GIZ Namibia’s agricultural business and capacity development project says farmers would normally reduce livestock numbers through sales, but FMD restrictions have limited this option. “Unfortunately, the livestock sector will now be hit heavily because the key strategy of destocking and marketing will not work,” he says. Hess says farmers should consider alternatives such as harvesting grass and planting fodder where irrigation is available. “We had a very rich rainy season. Who has been harvesting grass? And now we’re fighting for the dry grass that is out there,” he says. Food and Agriculture Organisation in Namibia programme support intern Oscar Kangwiya says Namibia should activate its disaster preparedness systems instead of waiting for conditions to worsen. “I know as a country we have a system, and it’s just a matter of us getting it ready and activated,” he says. Namibia Nature Foundation chairperson Mareike Voigts says farmers need clear information to decide what to produce and where to invest. “I still think knowledge or information is key so that farmers in this country really know what is expected and so they can make an informed decision,” she says. Voigts also calls for efficient water use, particularly where farmers rely on irrigation. “We really have to ensure we use that water efficiently and that we avoid any drainage of water. We must make sure the water stays where the roots can access it,” she says.

headline: Beekeepers want Animal Health Act to cover bees
body: Namibia faces a gap in detecting and managing bee diseases because bees are not adequately covered by the country’s animal health system. The issue was raised at the national apiculture role-player workshop held in Windhoek recently. The workshop brought together government officials, beekeepers, farmers, researchers, honey traders, training institutions and other role-players who discussed challenges facing the sector. The workshop aimed to review the laws and policies governing beekeeping, clarify the responsibilities of government institutions and identify gaps affecting the industry. The discussions are expected to contribute towards a National Apiculture Framework. Beekeeping Association of Namibia managing director Gretchen Burmeister says Namibia already has laws that could be used to regulate bee health, but gaps remain in their implementation. “The main thing is we already have an act that looks at the things that are connected to world trade, and the world health that we are obliged to keep,” she says. Burmeister says international bodies, including the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), recognise bees as animals when dealing with animal health and disease. “We are, since last year, obligated as a country to put bees under animals,” she says. She says this means bee diseases should also be dealt with under Namibia’s animal health laws. Burmeister says Namibia does not necessarily need a separate law for bees. “We already have an act; it is the regulations and the implementation, so to have another act is not actually required, but rather certain bodies that should be more substantiated or supported, both in the government and with the private sector,” she says. Burmeister adds that veterinarians and beekeepers need specialised training to improve the detection and management of bee diseases. Environmental Lawyers Network of Namibia chairperson Des-Rose Englebrecht says the Animal Health Act already provides a legal foundation that could be used to deal with issues such as bee diseases, movement, biosecurity and food control. “The problem, however, is that the act has not been properly operationalised for the agriculture sector, which is inclusive of various types of needs, and not just land communities, which is the main focus,” Englebrecht says. She says Namibia should also make use of existing African Union guidelines on beekeeping instead of developing a system from scratch. “The question is, why are we not using and implementing the framework that was specifically developed for the African conditions?” she questions She says a national mechanism is needed to bring the different institutions and role-players together. “The current fragmented approach is not producing any coherent outcomes for the sector,” Englebrecht says. Director of forestry Johnson Ndokosho says the Forest Act mainly refers to honey-producing organisms, which creates uncertainty over the protection of bees and other pollinators. “There are only two sections that are speaking about honey-producing organisms. “So, when discussing bees and honey-producing organisms, it’s important to note that some bees do not produce honey. You know that. What about those bees? They are not protected,” he says. Ndokosho says another problem is uncertainty over which government institution should handle different aspects of bee management. “The other challenge that we do know about, certainly, is that of coordination and lack of clarity,” Ndokosho says. He says forestry and agriculture authorities have previously discussed where responsibility for bee management should fall, given the role bees play in agriculture and food production. Ndokosho says the discussions led to efforts to establish a task team to look at bee management across government institutions.

headline: Agribank to assess FMD-hit farmers for repayment relief
body: Agribank says it will consider alternative repayment arrangements for farmers and agricultural businesses affected by the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, but will assess each case individually. The announcement comes after the government confirmed an FMD outbreak on a commercial farm in the ||Kharas region on 23 September, prompting restrictions on the movement and marketing of cloven-hoofed animals and animal products. Agricultural Bank of Namibia (Agribank) chief executive Robert Eiman says the restrictions could put pressure on farmers who are unable to sell or move livestock while still having to meet their financial obligations. “The bank is deeply concerned about the impact that these restrictions may have on its clients,” Eiman says. However, he cautions that the impact would differ between farmers and agricultural enterprises, meaning support would not automatically be extended to all affected clients. “Therefore, any support to be extended to our clients will not follow a one-size-fits-all approach; each request will be assessed on a case-by-case basis, considering the client’s circumstances,” he says. Agribank says affected clients should approach the bank to discuss how the outbreak and resulting restrictions have affected their operations. The approach could provide some breathing room for farmers whose cash flow has been disrupted by the restrictions, particularly where livestock sales have been delayed or halted. However, the bank did not specify what repayment options could be made available to affected borrowers, such as payment holidays, loan restructuring or extensions. The bank says clients affected by the restrictions can approach their nearest or preferred Agribank branch for assistance.

headline: Simon Jr vies for WBO, IBF Africa titles
body: Namibian boxer Harry Simon Jr will challenge Ghana’s Habib Giwa for the vacant WBO and IBF Africa welterweight titles at Rundu on 21 November. The MTC Nestor Sunshine Tobias Boxing and Fitness Academy this week announced the monumental night of professional boxing, co-headlined by one of the world’s most exciting prospects, Simon Jr. Boxing promoter Nestor Tobias says the title fight will mark a definitive step towards world title contention as Simon Jr challenges Giwa for the WBO and IBF Africa welterweight titles at the Rundu Trade Fair Hall. “Harry Simon Jr remains one of the most exceptional talents in boxing today. His momentum is at an all-time high following his last outing on 9 May 2026, where he delivered a spectacular fifth round knockout on the undercard of the WBO Global Super Bantamweight title event. “This upcoming bout marks his first major international title challenge, a milestone the academy believes will serve as a springboard to a future world title,” Tobias says. “I have shared a long-standing and productive relationship with Simon Jr. I have always rated him as a premier prospect, and I am incredibly excited to see him co-headline this championship fight.” Tobias says Simon Jr is a household name across Namibia, and they invite the nation to Rundu to witness the crowning of “a new king” in the welterweight division. He says the night promises to be one of the biggest in Namibian sporting history, featuring a stacked card with five international titles on the line. The confirmed bouts include the co-main event which features Martin ‘Alligator’ Mukungu vs Siphosethu Mvula (South Africa), Fillipus ‘Energy’ Nghitumbwa vs Ayabonga Sonjica, Mateus ‘The Beast’ Heita vs Ismael Kadri (South Africa), while the supporting bout will feature Paulinus ‘Jon Jon’ Ndjolonimu, with his opponent still to be announced. “We are determined to keep these titles in Namibia and believe this event will be a significant moment of national pride,” Tobias says. Interested persons will pay N$100 for general admission, while VIP tables seating 10 people will cost N$20 000.

headline: Namaseb wants Desert Jewels world cup-ready
body: Desert Jewels conditioning coach Charles Namaseb says Namibia must use the next 10 months wisely to prepare for the 2027 World Netball Cup in Australia. The Namibian sport fraternity has for ages been accused of sitting on its laurels until the very last minute instead of preparing national teams for international competitions in time. The trend is sport administrators wait a few weeks before the actual competition to kick start with earnest preparation, a situation seen by many sport critics as self inflicting. The Desert Jewels qualified for the world netball spectacle set for 25 August 2027 to 5 September 2027, alongside African giants Uganda, South Africa and Malawi. Namaseb tellsThe Namibian Sportthat though the world netball showdown is in August next year, having enough time to prepare will always be an advantage. “Having time is an advantage, but only if it’s used in stages. “The mistake would be to peak too early or to train hard without a plan. We build the foundation first, then add speed and power, then specificity, and finally sharpen and taper so the players arrive fresh.” Namaseb says they need to keep the players healthy, as an injury in March can cost more than a missed session. He says players who are based away from the national camp will have individual programmes, with regular check-ins and testing windows. “Consistency over the next 10 months matters more than any single hard session,” he says. LESSONS LEARNED- AFRICA CUP “A few themes stand out such as fatigue management across a tournament. Back-to-back matches showed that recovery is as important as training. “Finishing strongly. Late-game intensity and decision-making are won in the preparation phase. Squad depth and rotating players well means everyone must be conditioned to the same standard, not just the starters.” “Travel and adaptation. A long trip to Australia brings jet lag, different conditions and disrupted routines, so we’ll plan for it carefully.” Namaseb says the physical level will rise, as the opponents at the world cup will be faster and stronger. “So our speed, strength and contact-readiness targets must be higher than they were at continental level. Other specific observations from the tournament are at the quarters where intensity dropped.” On the macrocycle over the next 10 months, Namaseb says it runs in five blocks. “Within this, we use shorter mesocycles of three to four weeks with a lighter week for recovery, and we schedule testing at the end of each block so we can adjust the plan based on data. “We’ll also plan to arrive in Australia early enough to manage the time difference of roughly eight hours.” Namaseb says netball is a game of repeated explosive efforts, including jumping, landing, sprinting, decelerating and changing direction, which are often late in the fourth quarter. “My job is to make sure the players’ bodies can deliver what the coach’s game plan demands.” “The best tactics don’t help if a player is fatigued or injured. I see my role as two-fold: to raise performance and to keep players available. I work closely with the head coach, physiotherapist, doctor and nutritionist, because conditioning only works when everyone is pulling in the same direction.” He says his priorities are aerobic and repeated-sprint capacity so players can perform at high intensity across four quarters and several games. Footwork faults often show up when players are tired or rushed, so they train landing control and balance under fatigue, he adds. “The aim is for players to step onto the court for the last match of the tournament feeling close to how they did in the first.” “Every position has a different physical profile, so we individualise within the team framework.” Namaseb says centres, wing attack and wing defence (mid-court) cover the most distance and change pace constantly. “Their programme emphasises aerobic capacity, repeated-sprint ability and agility, with strength work aimed at maintaining power and protecting joints under high running volume.”

headline: Blockbuster Indoor Hockey Test Series in store
body: Namibian sport fans are in for a treat this weekend when African powerhouses, Namibia and South Africa (SA) square off in a five-match indoor hockey women’s test series in the capital. There has been little to separate the two sides in recent years, and with Namibia currently ranked eighth in the world and SA ninth, the series could go down to the wire. In their last encounter at the Nkosi Cup last year, SA beat Namibia 5-3, but Namibia won the Nkosi Cup in 2023 and 2024, beating SA on both occasions, while Namibia came sixth at the 2025 Indoor Hockey World Cup in Croatia and SA eighth. Both squads are well balanced with experienced stalwarts and exciting newcomers. For Namibia, goalkeeper Petro Stoffberg is the most experienced with 83 caps, while captain Sunelle Pretorius has 70, Gillian Hermanus 58, Azaylee Philander 47 and Jivanka Kruger 38. Some of the upcoming youngsters who are all still in their teens include Ottilie Hinda and the Grögli sisters Leila and Tamara; as well as Abigail Rowles and Anri Jacobs, who will make their international debuts. Jamie Southgate is SA’s most experienced player with 111 caps, while Edith Molikoe has 85 and Tegan Fourie 81. They are followed by Malikah Hamza (36), Sarah Paget (27), Cailynn den Bakker (24) and Bonolo Moabi (20), while Judie Blows, Jehan Abrahams, Manisha Desai and Anja Tromp will be making their debuts. Namibia coach Shayne Cormack says the series was initiated to help the teams prepare for the next Indoor Hockey World Cup in 2029. “This is part of our preparation for the world cup, and myself and SA coach Calvin Price have made a commitment to keep playing each other so that we can keep Africa hockey well developed for the world stage. So we made a commitment that we try and play each other once a year outside of the Nkosi Cup, because that’s a different tournament,” she says. “It’s a great opportunity to expose our younger players and less experienced players, and get more caps for them, because going forward we will need that experience if we want to qualify for the world cup,” she adds. Cormack says the series will provide a good test and strengthen competition for places in the side. “Some of the youngsters also played at the Nkosi Cup last year and they really made us proud, so we are excited to see what they can deliver. Then there are quite a few senior players who were not at the Nkosi Cup and actually haven’t played internationally for close to two years since the world cup, so we’ll see what their form is like,” she says. Namibia, however, will be without their inspirational captain Kiana Cormack, who is still recovering from brain surgery to have a tumour removed. “Kiana is recovering well, she will have another brain scan at the end of the month, but she has been tumour free for three months. So now she just has to heal and we hope that she can get back onto the court as soon as possible,” Cormack says. Cormack says she expects a close series. “It’s going to be a nice challenge. I don’t know what’s going to happen but Im just excited to try out a few things, to see what he’s going to try, and this will just help us grow as a team,” she says. “I think it’s going to be a great contest and I think it will be very competitive. I’m not going to worry too much about the results – obviously we want to win games and we want to breed a winning culture, but we are now at a stage where we are trying to give our less experienced players more exposure and hopefully by the next Nkosi Cup, we’ll be at the next level,” she says. The test series will be held at the Sports Facilitation Centre at the Windhoek Showgrounds, with the first test at 18h00 tomorrow, to be followed by two tests on Saturday and two on Sunday.

headline: Dressage riders converge at Okahandja for championships
body: Dressage riders gather at Okahandja from Thursday for the 2026 FEI Dressage World Challenge, the 7 Nations Challenge and the 2026 Namibian Dressage Championships. The 2025 Namibian champions Svenja Späth and her stallion Equimaster Seeis Arian hope to excel on home ground, with their performance at the same venue a month ago indicating that Arian is back on form after his prolonged absence. Also setting out to retain their title is the 2025 junior champion Leia-Mae van der Merwe on F.H.M. The talented and dedicated youngster from Windhoek has little to fear in serious local competition, but she will be hoping to improve on her performance at last year’s FEI Dressage World Challenge, where she came 18th out of about 100 riders competing at youth level in their respective countries. Also out to score big in the FEI Challenge is Carolin Hoffmeister. She ranked eighth out of 117 competitors in the senior category on Batman in 2025. This year she will be concentrating on uplifting her performance with Heidi’s Mohinho in the Senior II Class. The veterinary inspection, team announcements and FEI draw will take place at the Reitclub Okahandja premises tomorrow afternoon as of 16h00, while the FEI classes start at 11h00 on Friday, with the 7 Nations classes set for later in the afternoon. The competitions counting towards the Namibian Championships begin at 08h00 on Saturday morning, while the best in musical freestyles will be showcased in the main arena at 09h00 on Sunday morning with, the final prize giving ceremony at 13h15.

headline: Keetmanshoop man arrested for killing girlfriend
body: A man (39) has been arrested at Keetmanshoop for allegedly killing his girlfriend during a fight and for allegedly possessing cannabis. National police spokesperson deputy commissioner Kauna Shikwambi, in a police report released on Sunday, says the incident occurred at about 09h40 on Saturday at a house in Ileni location. The couple allegedly had an argument which escalated into a physical fight, during which the suspect allegedly killed his girlfriend. The deceased, Wilhelmina Waterboer (39), was declared dead when an ambulance arrived at the scene. “No visible injuries or open wounds were detected on the body of the deceased, the suspicion is internal injuries,” Shikwambi says. She says the suspect was arrested and during his arrest and detention, the police allegedly found him in possession of one bankie of cannabis. The value of the cannabis has not yet been determined. Waterboer’s body was transported to the Keetmanshoop mortuary pending autopsy. The police say the suspect is expected to appear in the Keetmanshoop Magistrate’s Court on Monday. Shikwambi says Waterboer’s next of kin have been informed and police investigation continues. Meanwhile, the police have arrested a teenager (19) at Rundu after attempting to murder a man (36) at Ndama area in the Kavango East region on Friday. The incident allegedly occurred at about 21h00 at Tumweneneni location, where the teenager and another suspect allegedly attacked the man with knives. “The two suspects used knives to stab a 36-year-old Namibian male complainant several times on the back and caused serious injuries,” she says. The victim was taken to Rundu Intermediate Hospital and is in a serious condition. One of the suspects allegedly fled the scene and remains at large. Police investigations into both incidents are continuing. In another incident, two women aged 50 and 26 were arrested at Oshakati on Friday after they were found selling controlled wildlife products without a valid permit. The police say they recovered items including jewellery and other items made out of elephant tusks. Shikwambi says the value is not yet determined. Police investigation continues.

headline: Lawyer Conradie sentenced to pay N$200 000 fine on corruption charges
body: Veteran lawyer Dirk Conradie has been sentenced to pay a fine of N$200 000 or serve a five-year prison term on two charges under the Anti-Corruption Act on which he was found guilty in February. Conradie and a co-accused, Sara Damases, were sentenced in the Windhoek High Court on Monday. Judge Thomas Masuku found Conradie and Damases guilty on counts of corruptly soliciting gratification as a reward for using influence in procuring a contract, and attempting or conspiring to contravene sections of the Anti-Corruption Act. He found that Conradie solicited gratification from the directors of an advertising company, DV8 Saatchi & Saatchi, during a meeting at the offices of his law firm, Conradie & Damaseb, in Windhoek in June 2012. Conradie did so by asking the advertising company’s directors to agree to take Damases on board in their business as a black economic empowerment partner or in any other role, while promising that in return he would use his influence with the board of directors of the company Mobile Telecommunications Limited (MTC), of which he was the chairperson, to ensure an advertising contract worth about N$60 million would be awarded to DV8. Masuku sentenced Damases to pay a fine of N$60 000 or serve a prison term of two years. He said he considered that Conradie abused his position as chairperson of the MTC board of directors. Neither Conradie nor Damases benefited personally from the scheme in which they were involved, though, Masuku noted.

headline: Woman suffers serious burns after attack
body: A woman was seriously burned after a suspect allegedly kicked a pot of boiling porridge at her during an argument at Mutjiku village in the Kavango East region, on Thursday. This was announced in the weekend crime report by national police spokesperson deputy commissioner Kauna Shikwambi. “It is alleged that during an argument, the suspect kicked a pot of boiling porridge at the victim, causing serious burns to her face, hands and legs,” she says. Shikwambi says the victim has been admitted to the hospital for treatment, while the suspect has been arrested and remains in police custody.Police investigation are continuing.

headline: Woman arrested for drugs worth N$2.2m at Goreagab
body: A Namibian woman (38) has been arrested after police seized cannabis and Mandrax tablets worth more than N$2.2 million at Goreagab, Windhoek, on Saturday. National police spokesperson deputy commissioner Kauna Shikwambi says the drugs were seized during a police search. ”About 10 215 grams of suspected cannabis and 17 717 suspected Mandrax tablets,” Shikwambi says. The woman is facing charges under the Abuse of Dependency-Producing Substances and Rehabilitation Centres Act for allegedly dealing in prohibited dependency-producing substances, as well as a charge under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act.
